Episode details

Could AI have solved mathematics’ greatest mystery? The Riemann Hypothesis has baffled mathematicians for 165 years, but mathematician Levent Alpoge believes he has found a proof, working with AI system Claude. Tom Whipple and mathematician Kit Yates explore what this could mean for mathematics and the humans who dedicate their lives to it. Plus, head to the University of Reading to discover how an Allosaurus ate its prey. With the help of a contraption called Dinosaw and a roast chicken, Manabu Sakamoto is trying to understand how the teeth of these prehistoric predators cut through flesh. Produced in partnership with The Open University. item.title: JWST studies a tiny, metal-poor galaxy with just a fraction of the sun's oxygen abundance
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

November 26, 2026 report

JWST studies a tiny, metal-poor galaxy with just a fraction of the sun's oxygen abundance

Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have studied one of the most metal-poor galaxies known. Seen as it was around 12.2 billion years ago, LAP2 is a tiny system with a stellar mass comparable to that of a massive star cluster. The research paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Nov. 3.

Poor in metals

Early galaxies have very little metal, and over time they build up metals. Observations show that a galaxy's metal content is linked to its mass in stars—a relationship known as the mass-metallicity relation.

JWST is now spotting a class of galaxies in the first billion years of the universe, called extremely metal-poor galaxies (EMPGs). These galaxies have only a few percent of the sun's metals or less, and they serve as natural laboratories to trace the earliest stages of star formation and galaxy evolution.

Astronomers have noticed that some of these early galaxies are more metal-poor than local relations predict. A few approach the regime of 'metal-free' systems made of pristine gas with only hydrogen and helium and no heavier elements. They offer conditions expected for Population III stars, the first stars to have formed in the universe from pristine gas. The gas lit up by such stars is predicted to show very weak oxygen lines and strong helium (He II) emission.

These galaxies are, however, very faint and Population III stars are short-lived, making them rare and hard to spot. Many of the best candidates are therefore seen through gravitational lensing. That's when the light from a distant object is magnified by a massive foreground object.

Oxygenless candidate

LAP2 was first identified in MUSE observations in 2021. It is a very faint galaxy, but is strongly magnified, roughly 50 times, by a foreground galaxy cluster called Abell 2744. This allows astronomers to examine its structure and chemical composition. When they first looked at it with the JWST, they detected no sign of oxygen at all. But that first look only covered a small part of the galaxy, so they were not so sure of the result.

In this new study, astronomers led by Matteo Messa of the INAF Astrophysics and Space Science Observatory of Bologna revisit LAP2 with JWST's NIRSpec integral field spectroscopy, which captures both lensed images in full.

The team found no oxygen signal in the new full-galaxy data. The method for turning line strength into an oxygen amount has never been used at such low levels, so the numbers are extrapolations and carry real uncertainty. Even then, LAP2 was found to have less than about 0.5% of the sun's oxygen. This placed it among the lowest ever measured but still above the expected levels for Population III star formation.

"The non-detection of [O iii]λ5007 in the integrated spectrum confirms LAP2 as an oxygen-deficient system…" as first suggested by the previous study, the team writes in the paper. The team says its light is consistent with a very metal-poor star, possibly mixed with some pristine gas.

Varying chemistry

The faint oxygen appeared only from the small, dense core, whereas the rest of the galaxy showed no signal. There may be two reasons for this. First, the harsh conditions of the dense core may simply make its oxygen glow brighter, even if the core has the same oxygen as the rest of the galaxy. Alternatively, the core probably made its own oxygen. This requires only 0.2 solar masses of oxygen produced by exploding stars.

By modeling the galaxy's colors and emission lines using the NIRCam imaging and spectrum, the team estimated the galaxy's stellar mass. It turned out to be around 80,000 solar masses, which is comparable to that of massive star clusters found in the local and distant universe.

"LAP2 is among the most metal-poor galaxies known to date and one of the few with a stellar mass comparable to that of individual star clusters," the team writes.

Colors combined with emission lines revealed the best-fit age of the stars to be around 7 million years. It also appeared to be undergoing a recent, dust-free burst of star formation.

Fairly empty region

A quick look at its surroundings showed that LAP2 sits in a fairly empty region with a few neighbors. LAP2 lies between two groups of galaxies. The team says that isolation like this protects gas from being polluted by nearby galaxies' winds. "This lets pockets of nearly pristine gas survive well after reionization, as predicted by models of late Pop III star formation," the team explains.

This isolation supports LAP2 as a site of pristine star formation at a redshift of 4, around 1.5 billion years after the Big Bang. The team notes that the galaxy catalog is uneven, so a proper measure of its isolation was not possible.

Although its chemistry varies across the galaxy, LAP2 is still extremely low in oxygen, which makes it one of the purest regions among such galaxies. The team says that with new diagnostics and spectroscopic follow-ups, the number of extremely metal-poor galaxy candidates is expected to grow, which would open an even wider window into early-universe star formation and galaxy evolution.

You'll get an ad-free account as a thank-you.

item.title: Inside the Hot Wheels Design Center
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Excerpted from HOT WHEELS: THE CREATIVE DRIVE: Imagination and Innovation at the Hot Wheels Design Center by Dan Bova and Freddie Holmes. HOT WHEELS™ and associated trademarks and trade dress are owned by Mattel. Reprinted by permission of Mattel Press.

Inside the Hot Wheels Design Center

“Those are some Hot Wheels!”

State-of-the-art car garage. Museum. Mad scientist’s lab. Stuntworks. The most incredible toy store on Earth—Mattel’s Handler Team Center, the company’s design hub tucked away on a nondescript stretch of road in El Segundo, California—is all these things and more.

From a giant mural, Mattel’s cofounders, Elliot and Ruth Handler, smile down on the building’s front lobby, where life-size Hot Wheels vehicles appear poised for action, and wall art displays iconic Mattel playsets and characters from the company’s inception through the present day. Down at the very far end of the lobby, the Epic Loop screams for attention. It is an eleven-foot-tall Hot Wheels duo racetrack with side-by-side loops. Visitors are encouraged to re-create a game played by millions of young Hot Wheels fans by climbing a flight of stairs and sending a die-cast car of their choice down the competing tracks in a race to launch their car into a bucket that marks the finish line.

There’s speed (the cars reach what would equate to 297 mph at full scale), experimentation (do you go with a weightier or sleeker car?), and crashes. Lots of crashes.

The message is clear: This place is a temple of wild design and outrageous fun.

Push deeper into the 200,000-square-foot building (which once housed an aerospace company), and you arrive at the beating heart of the world’s most famous brand on four wheels: the Hot Wheels Design Center.

Every inch of this place is filled with reminders of Hot Wheels’ storied past, as well as the schematics and prototypes that map out its high-tech future.

Oh, and there are toy cars. Everywhere. Toy cars on tables, toy cars in pristine display cases fit for the Louvre, smashed-up toy cars piled in cluttered cubicles. It’s every kid’s and every collector’s dream come true—as well as a dream come true for the people working inside these walls.

“We Start Wild”

The Hot Wheels die-cast design team sits together in a ring, their cubicles surrounding long tables that serve as a communal space for collaboration, display, tinkering, and sharing the occasional Friday morning donut.

Black light-blocking hoods arch over each cubicle, giving them the feeling of a custom car garage or the messiest kid’s bedroom ever. Within the cubicles, toy cars in every stage of design are piled up against keyboards, and the interior cube walls are plastered with pinned-up artwork, schematics, and toy racks.

Underneath one of these hoods sits Dwayne Vance, a longtime Hot Wheels designer who is now manager of product design and steers the visual direction of every graphic in die-cast for Hot Wheels. Vance has worked for other huge brands like DC Comics, EA Games, and Texaco, and his passion for art and automotive extends well beyond the walls of this place, from his creation and curation of art shows to his own book series, Masters of Chicken Scratch, devoted to futuristic and fantasy hot-rod artwork and designs.

An oversize rendering he created in the early 2000s of the Hot Wheels classic car Bone Shaker, with the word Attitude boldly emblazoned across the top, hangs over his work area. Unlike many of his fellow designers, Vance’s cubicle is neatly arranged and organized. “It helps me creatively to sit down in a nice clean space,” he says. Some of his favorite cars fill his shelves, as does his Matty Award.

Every designer has particular strengths, so when Hot Wheels decided it was time to breathe new life into the Custom Camaro, Vance was part of a small group of designers tasked with cooking up new concepts. “We wanted a licensed vehicle but with an extreme custom,” says Staff Product Designer Fraser Campbell. “Knowing Dwayne’s work, I knew he’d create something wild.”

As pens hit paper in a flurry of ideas, the designers soon faced a challenge not uncommon for Hot Wheels: the ticking clock. Campbell explains that when putting together a year’s lineup for initial concept review (ICR), where the cars get evaluated and refined to ensure a good overall mix before things move along to production, the designers need to fill in any perceived gaps—quickly.

“Several of us designers were going to be working on the Camaro, but the other guys got so busy that it was up to me to finish the project,” says Vance. “So, I was like, ‘Okay, cool!’ I got to spend maybe two weeks on the design—it wasn’t a lot. One thing we don’t have here is the luxury of time.”

But just like race car drivers behind the wheels of the cars they’re inspired by, Hot Wheels designers thrive under pressure.

Getting in Gear

Vance began where he always begins—sketching. “I usually just go straight to Photoshop. I have a monitor on my desk, and I actually sketch right on the monitor,” he explains. But the motor muse can strike at any time and any place, and in the case of this redesign, it hit Vance at thirty thousand feet.

“I was on a plane and pulled out my sketchbook and put down some initial ideas,” he says. He typically has a sketchbook within reach, but any piece of paper will do. “Sometimes I’ll draw a little piece of a car on a sticky note,” he says.

Whenever the muse speaks, he listens—and gives it a soundtrack with the help of a little music and his headphones. “I listen to a lot of deep house when I’m drawing in my cube,” he says. “It’s got good energy and is easy to draw to.”…

item.title: Wave-like displays in animal groups may have evolved to deceive predators
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Wave-like displays in animal groups may have evolved to deceive predators

Some of the most striking patterns in collective behavior emerge in the face of danger. When a predator approaches, some animal groups morph into a vision of pulsing waves. These patterns might be more than a side effect of group living; they could have evolved as a form of deception, argue Dr. Eduardo Sampaio and professor Iain Couzin of the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior (MPI-AB) and the University of Konstanz in a Perspectives piece published in Science.

For example, when a peregrine falcon attacks European starlings, dark bands sweep through the flock roughly every three-quarters of a second. In the sulfur-rich springs of Mexico, mollies in dense schools repeatedly dive and resurface, creating waves of motion that fend off predators. Giant honeybees shimmer their abdomens, propagating waves across the nest that drive away hornets.

"We propose that these collective displays exploit how predators see motion, confusing or misleading them," says Sampaio, who is a postdoctoral researcher at MPI-AB.

Nature abounds in collective animal motion, like flocking, schooling and swarming. Yet few studies have ever looked at these group patterns from the outside, through the eyes of a predator. The authors draw together disparate examples—starling murmurations, fish waves, honeybee shimmering—and present the common effect that those patterns can have on the eyes watching them.

In each case, the wave pattern travels faster than the animals producing it, repeats and often anticipates the strike of a predator. The trick is not limited to groups of prey: a hunting cuttlefish sends similar moving stripes down its own body, which may hide its approach from crabs.

"These systems might look different on the surface, but in each one we see the same decoupling of the collective pattern from the motion of the body, or bodies, that generate it," says Couzin, who is a director of collective behavior at MPI-AB and a professor at the University of Konstanz.

These collective waves may exploit the limits of how motion can be processed in the brain. By misleading biological vision, the pattern generators have better chances of survival. And this, the authors say, opens the door to natural selection. They outline how natural selection can act on individual-level rules, like how sensitive each animal is to its neighbors or its response threshold. These are heritable traits. How they vary can alter the effect on the predator, and therefore each individual's survival.

The next challenge is to test these ideas experimentally. Do these patterns simply happen to impair predators—in other words, are they just a lucky side effect—or did they evolve because they do? New experimental tools now make it possible to find out.

Computer models of animal vision, virtual reality and neural recordings allow researchers to test which features of the display actually affect predators. For example, the timing and coordination of collective responses can be adjusted while group size and density are kept constant. "Such experiments could reveal whether the timing of collective waves deters or deceives predators more effectively than fleeing alone does," says Sampaio.

Publication details

Eduardo Sampaio et al., Deception in motion, Science (2026). DOI: 10.1126/science.aek0041. www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aek0041

Journal information: Science

item.title: Runaway pulsar escapes the remnant of its own supernova
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

November 26, 2026 feature

Runaway pulsar escapes the remnant of its own supernova

A team of astronomers has spotted a rare example of a pulsar that has escaped the cloud of debris left by the supernova explosion in which it formed. Led by Rohit Dokara, formerly at the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy, the team made the discovery by chance, adding to just a handful of similar known cases.

The team's discovery suggests that many similar observations could soon be made with new generations of radio telescopes: perhaps helping astronomers to solve unanswered questions surrounding the origins of fast-moving pulsars and the surprising sparsity of supernova remnants within the galaxy.

Their results have been accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics and are currently available on the arXiv preprint server.

Missing pulsars

A pulsar is a highly magnetized, rapidly rotating neutron star that emits powerful beams of radiation from each of its poles. If one of these beams happens to point in Earth's direction, it will appear to astronomers as an intense electromagnetic flash pulsing with striking regularity, much like the beam from a lighthouse.

These strange bodies form when the cores of massive stars collapse in supernova explosions, which also blast out immense clouds of gas and dust called supernova remnants (SNRs). Each cloud forms a rapidly expanding shell, which thins out and dissipates into interstellar space within around 100,000 years.

Yet for reasons astronomers are still working to fully understand, the pulsar itself will often receive a powerful kick during the initial explosion, propelling it away from the center of the expanding cloud. As it plows through the surrounding gas, it can leave behind a comet-like tail.

In some rare cases, this kick is particularly extreme. "As far as I know, there are four cases where, after a core-collapse supernova explosion, a pulsar has formed moving faster than the diffuse ejecta that eventually becomes a shell," Dokara explains. "Such cases offer unique views of some of the fastest compact objects in our galaxy."

Alongside the mystery of these kicks, there are also unanswered questions surrounding the abundance of SNRs within the galaxy. Astronomers estimate that roughly 2,000 SNRs should exist in the Milky Way—but to date, only around 400 have ever been discovered.

Combined surveys

In their study, Dokara's team initially aimed to investigate this discrepancy using combined observations from several large-scale radio surveys, carried out by radio telescopes around the world over the past two decades and across a broad range of frequencies. These surveys capture radio waves created by electrons spiraling through magnetic fields within an SNR's expanding shell and can also reveal pulsars and their tails.

Combined with existing timing measurements of pulsars, this data allowed the astronomers to calculate three key factors for any pulsar–SNR pair. First, by measuring the rate at which the pulsar's spin is slowing down (as determined by precisely timing its pulses), they could roughly calculate its age. Second, by measuring the angular separation between the pulsar and the center of the shell in the radio images, they could work out how far apart the two appear on the sky.

Finally, they accounted for how lower-frequency radio waves are slowed down more by free electrons in their path—which are thinly spread through interstellar space. By measuring the delay in arrival time between radio waves with higher and lower frequencies, the team could estimate the pulsar's distance from Earth and, by extension, the SNR's.

From these three factors, Dokara's team could estimate both the pulsar's velocity and the SNR's size and evolutionary state—indicating where it lies along its transformation from the initial supernova to a fully dissipated cloud.

Chance discovery

While combing through the data, Dokara uncovered an association that had previously gone unnoticed. "By chance, I found a new supernova remnant shell and a known pulsar to be well outside this shell, but with its tail very clearly pointing to the center of the shell," he says. "We estimated its transverse velocity to be over 1,400 kilometers per second (870 miles per second), making it one of the largest values for Milky Way pulsars."

Since the new shell and the pulsar's tail were first spotted in images from MeerKAT—one of the latest generation of radio telescopes—the discovery holds promising implications for the observational abilities of newer facilities. With their improved sensitivity and resolution, the team now hopes that similar observations could appear regularly in future large-scale surveys.

"The science potential for each such survey is enormous, and this work is just one small example of combining data from such surveys using standard methods to discover and identify rare associations," Dokara adds.

Source: Phys.org | Published: 2026-11-26 18:50 UTC

item.title: Second court defeat for Trump's deep-sea mining ambitions
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Second court defeat for Trump's deep-sea mining ambitions

The Trump administration's plans to begin deep-sea mining in the Pacific have hit a second legal setback after a federal judge ruled plans to lease areas of sea-floor off the Northern Mariana Islands violated the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

The court's decision follows a similar ruling over a proposed lease sale off American Samoa.

Opposition groups who lodged the Northern Mariana Islands lawsuit said they were concerned deep-sea mining could cause long-term damage to the ocean ecosystem.

The US government has said it wants to start deep-sea mining to enable access to critical minerals and to counter China's growing influence over crucial components needed for electronics.

The administration had planned to put up for sale leases for the Northern Mariana Islands on 16 December 2026.

It is not clear what will happen next as the administration chose not to recognise the first court ruling and went ahead with the sale of two leases covering 13 million hectares (more than 30 million acres) off American Samoa.

Opponents have vowed to challenge that sale.

Ruling on the Northern Mariana Islands case, District judge Jill Aiko Otake said the defendants, the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), which provided the expert opinion behind the lease sales, and Howard Lutnick, who was named in his capacity as head of the department that oversees the agency, had failed to consider the potential effects that could follow once the leases were issued.

The ruling explained that while these leases would only authorise the leaseholder to conduct preliminary surveying activity, they might eventually allow the leaseholder to actually mine the ocean's floor.

The potential impact of that mining had not been addressed in the biodiversity assessment which was used to sign off the lease sales, the ruling said.

Using machines to mine for minerals in the deep ocean is highly controversial.

Some scientists have raised concerns that deep-sea mining could damage little-understood deep-ocean ecosystems, though industry supporters argue the environmental effects remain uncertain and require further study.

Deep-sea mining uses vacuum technology to suck up nodules from the muddy sediment., external However, this process also removes organisms that grow on them, including corals and sponges, many of which cannot grow anywhere else.

In one study of the impact of deep-sea mining, researchers found more than 4,000 animals, 90% of which were new species, living on the seafloor in a remote area of the Pacific Ocean.

Some critics of the industry fear that before we have the chance to explore the full nature of life in the undiscovered deep ocean, it could be endangered.

Norway was the first country in the world to approve commercial-scale deep-sea mining in 2024.

Over 2,000 of the world's scientists met in 2025 to review the data on ocean health and they recommended governments halt deep sea exploration while further research on the impacts was carried out.

More than 30 countries supported this position and called for a moratorium.

Shortly before that meeting, President Trump published executive orders to push ahead with mining and "unleash America's offshore critical minerals and resources".

He said "these resources are key to strengthening our economy, securing our energy future, and reducing dependence on foreign suppliers for critical minerals".

Part of the plan aims to "counter China's growing influence over seabed mineral resources".

Deep-sea mining targets polymetallic nodules, external â potato-sized rocks found over 4,000 metres below the ocean surface.

These contain minerals including nickel, cobalt, and manganese which are used in manufactruring electronics and batteries.

They are also important for renewable energy technologies to tackle climate change, including solar panels, wind turbines and electric vehicles.

The International Energy Agency predicts that demand for the minerals could at least double by 2040., external
